correctness.rationale: During first n arrivals each agent receives at most one item, so deleting the envied singleton makes EF1 automatic. At time n every agent has a singleton. For earliest low-recipient j, each other agent i either got a high-valued singleton (thus maximal own value) or got a low-valued singleton later; in the latter case i was available when g_j arrived, so its nonselection under high-first means v_i(g_j)=ell_i=v_i(g_i). Thus j is universally unenvied. At the (n+1)st arrival place new good with j: any outside i can discard this new good and compare with j’s unenvied first singleton, while all other envied bundles remain singleton. If all n had high singleton, choose any anchor. All n, real positive tier sizes and m≤n+1 are covered. Independently exhausted 4160 binary high-low preference patterns for n=2 and n=3 with heterogeneous tiers and evaluated EF1 at every prefix; finite tests corroborate analytic anchor lemma only.

value.rationale: The first n goods can be allocated one per agent with automatic EF1, making the n+1st good the first substantive online fairness obstruction. A universally unenvied singleton anchor gives a sharp constructive positive result for heterogeneous two-tier preferences without lookahead or buffering.

final_claim: For all n≥2, streams of at most n+1 indivisible goods, and additive positive personalized two-tier values 0<ell_i<h_i, a deterministic irrevocable allocation rule maintains EF1 after every prefix without lookahead: first assign each good to an unassigned high-valuer if available, then give the sole surplus good to the earliest low-tier first recipient or any if none.
limitations: Tier constants per agent fixed and positive, every good immediately assigned, no general efficiency or EFX.
residual_risks: No guarantee for the second surplus good (m≥n+2), nonadditive or three-tier values.
An elementary first-surplus anchor may already occur as an unstated corollary in online fair-division literature.
